title: SLM Architecture
intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly transformed AI, powering applications such as chatbots, content generation, coding assistants, and intelligent search. However, bigger models often come with higher computational costs, infrastructure requirements, latency, and data-privacy concerns. This has created growing interest in Small Language Models (SLMs).

SLMs are language models with fewer parameters than traditional large models, designed to deliver efficient performance for specific tasks. Rather than trying to solve every possible problem, an SLM can be optimized for focused use cases such as text classification, summarization, information extraction, customer support, or domain-specific question answering.

sections.heading: What Makes a Model "Small"?
sections.body:
There is no universal parameter count that defines a Small Language Model (SLM). Generally, an SLM is significantly smaller and more resource-efficient than a Large Language Model (LLM), while still being capable of performing specific tasks effectively.

The most obvious measure is parameter count. Models with hundreds of millions to a few billion parameters are often considered small, depending on their architecture and intended use. However, parameter count alone doesn't determine whether a model is truly “small.”

Other factors include memory usage, inference speed, computational requirements, and deployment cost. A model that can run efficiently on a laptop, edge device, or local server may be considered small from a practical deployment perspective.

SLMs are also commonly optimized for specific tasks or domains, such as classification, summarization, information extraction, or customer support.

Ultimately, “small” is about more than model size. It means achieving the right balance between accuracy, performance, cost, and resource requirements for a particular use case.

sections.heading: Benefits of SLMs Over LLMs
sections.body:
• Lower Cost: SLMs require fewer computational resources, reducing infrastructure and inference costs, especially for high-volume applications.
  • Faster Response: Smaller models typically provide lower latency, making them suitable for real-time applications such as chatbots and intelligent assistants.
  • Lower Hardware Requirements: SLMs can run on smaller servers, laptops, and edge devices without requiring expensive GPU infrastructure.
  • Better Privacy: SLMs can be deployed locally or within private infrastructure, allowing sensitive data to remain within controlled environments.
  • Easier Customization: Smaller models can be fine-tuned efficiently for specific domains and tasks such as classification, summarization, and information extraction.
  • Energy Efficiency: SLMs generally require less computing power, resulting in lower energy consumption during inference.
  • Cost-Effective Scaling: Organizations can deploy multiple SLM instances for specialized tasks without the infrastructure costs associated with large models.

Overall, SLMs are a strong choice when speed, cost, privacy, and efficiency are more important than the broad capabilities of a large general-purpose model.
